claims.text: AlCrFeNiSi can be fabricated by binder-containing 3D ink-extrusion to form a green body followed by isothermal sintering.
Replacing high-energy beam AM with ink extrusion and isothermal sintering will minimize residual thermal stresses in AlCrFeNiSi components.
The proposed route will reduce processing complexity relative to conventional high-energy beam AM.
The proposed route will yield superior mechanical properties relative to conventional high-energy beam AM.
The starting AlCrFeNiSi feedstock is powder produced by gas atomization or a similar technique.
Conventional laser or electron-beam processing of AlCrFeNiSi produces high thermal gradients, residual stresses, and heterogeneous microstructures.
Ink-extruded and sintered miniature components can have features or filaments approximately 100 µm in size.
A sintering temperature near 1573 K is an applicable processing window for AlCrFeNiSi.
Processing under inert or vacuum conditions will limit oxidation.
Slow isothermal sintering will produce a uniformly densified, low-residual-stress microstructure with refined and consistent grain distributions.
Slow isothermal sintering promotes complete inter-particle diffusion while minimizing thermal gradients.
Avoiding rapid temperature changes reduces thermal strain and residual stress.
Binder-based printing permits near-net-shape formation with low processing complexity.
Controlled binder removal and gradual consolidation produce a homogeneous microstructure without defects common to high-energy AM.
Sintered binder-based components will have lower residual stress than laser-melted components.
Sintered binder-based components will have greater ductility and strength than laser-melted components.
Sintered binder-based components will exhibit less microstructural heterogeneity than laser-melted components.
The hypothesis may not apply at substantially larger component scales or to different feedstock compositions.

contradictions.description: The proposed intervention is specifically 3D ink-extrusion printing, but the predicted outcome and falsification rule refer to binder jetting. Binder jetting and ink extrusion are distinct binder-based AM processes, so the process being tested is not consistently identified.
